newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. growing concerned about Japan surplus-Gyohten.
newsitem.headline: U.S. growing concerned about Japan surplus-Gyohten.

text.p: The United States is growing concerned about Japan's trade surplus, Toyoo Gyohten, a former key Japanese Finance Ministry official, said on Thursday.
Gyohten said there was a "mismatch" of views regarding the Japanese economy between Japan and other countries, especially the United States.
"Particularly in Washington...I understand that there is growing concern about the (Japanese) trade surplus," Gyohten told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
He also said that, while there were views in Washington that Japan should try to accelerate growth through fiscal policies, there was no strong support in Tokyo for such measures.

Gyohten, a senior adviser to the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd and a former vice finance minister for international affairs, also said that neither the U.S. Treasury nor the Japanese Finance Ministry was unhappy with the present dollar/yen rate of about 110 yen.
"The current rate of around 110 yen will be one which does not make anybody terribly unhappy -- the U.S. Treasury and businesses or the Japanese Ministry of Finance and businesses," he said.

He said the yen's weakening since the latter half of 1995 was behind the recent rise in Tokyo's trade surplus but added that the surplus will not be a structural one as the yen has strengthened again since the spring of this year.

The former MOF official said the Group of Seven nations were likely to reaffirm the importance of stability in exchange rates and to reconfirm their pledge to cooperate to achieve that goal at the upcoming summit in Denver.
On the Japanese economy, Gyohten said he believed that there will be a credit tightening by the end of the year, pointing out that the economy is now on a recovery path.
But he said Japanese authorities would like to wait and see how the economy performed in the April-June quarter following a rise in the national consumption tax from April 1.
"That means August could be the earliest date for any reconsideration of monetary policy," Gyohten said, adding that economic data for the April-June period will have come out by then.
